title: Build, Run, and Inspect Your First Container
intro: Let's build an image, run it as a container, and poke at it — the core Docker loop you'll repeat constantly.

steps.prompt: Build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory, tagging it 'myapp:v1'.
steps.fake_output:
Step 1/5 : FROM node:20-alpine
 ---> a1b2c3d4
Step 5/5 : CMD ["node", "server.js"]
 ---> Running in e5f6g7h8
Successfully built i9j0k1l2
Successfully tagged myapp:v1
steps.explanation: Each Dockerfile instruction becomes a cached layer — this is why reordering COPY/RUN steps in a Dockerfile can drastically speed up rebuilds.
steps.why: Without -t, the image builds but gets an unmemorable hash as its only identifier — tagging it 'myapp:v1' is what lets every later command (run, push) refer to it by a name you'll actually remember.

steps.prompt: Run it in detached mode, mapping host port 8080 to container port 3000.
steps.explanation: -d runs it in the background and returns the container ID immediately.
steps.why: Without -d, the container runs in your foreground terminal and blocks it until you Ctrl+C (which stops the container) — -d is what you want for anything meant to keep running while you do other things.

steps.fake_output:
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       PORTS                    STATUS
7f3a9b2c1d0e   myapp:v1    0.0.0.0:8080->3000/tcp   Up 5 seconds
steps.explanation: docker ps only shows running containers — add -a to see stopped ones too.
steps.why: If a container crashed right after starting, plain 'docker ps' would show nothing and make it look like the run command silently failed — 'docker ps -a' is the one to reach for when a container you expect to see isn't showing up here.

steps.explanation: Same idea as kubectl logs — every container's stdout/stderr is captured here.
steps.why: Add -f to this to stream logs live, same as kubectl logs -f — the flag names lining up between Docker and Kubernetes isn't a coincidence, kubectl's CLI was deliberately modeled on Docker's for exactly this kind of muscle-memory transfer.

steps.prompt: Get a shell inside the running container.
steps.explanation: Alpine-based images usually only have /bin/sh, not bash — worth remembering when exec fails with 'executable file not found'.
steps.why: This is the exact same pattern as kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh — a container is a container whether Kubernetes is managing it or not, which is why the debugging technique transfers directly.
